plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a scene diagram of an airplane sighting two points on a straight highway below it. A small colored drawing of a jetliner sits at the upper left, nose pointed left, and a teal dashed horizontal line runs to the right from the aircraft to stand for the horizontal at flight altitude. Across the lower part of the figure a solid black horizontal line represents the highway, with two labeled points on it: A toward the middle and B at the far right. Two gray dashed sight lines drop from the airplane to those points, the line to A being the steeper of the pair and the line to B running much shallower because B lies farther off. Arcs drawn at the airplane mark the two angles opening downward from the dashed horizontal, labeled 25 degrees for the shallow line toward B and 49 degrees for the steep line toward A. Sharing a single vertex for both angles of depression turns the two sight lines and the road into a pair of triangles with a common side. The arrangement supports solving for the airplane's slant distance to A and its elevation above the road once the spacing between the two mileposts is supplied.

interactionPlan.concept: Angles of depression to two collinear points on the ground create two distinct right triangles that share the same vertical altitude, forming a system of equations.
elements: airplane graphic at upper left, facing right
teal dashed horizontal line representing flight altitude reference
solid black horizontal ground line
point A on the ground line (closer to plane)
point B on the ground line (farther from plane)
gray dashed sight line from airplane to point A
gray dashed sight line from airplane to point B
angle arc and label (e.g., 49°) from horizontal down to sight line A
angle arc and label (e.g., 25°) from horizontal down to sight line B
vertical dashed altitude line from airplane to ground (appears in later phases)
right angle squares at the base of the altitude line (appears in later phases)
alternate interior angle arcs at points A and B (appears in later phases)
labels for altitude 'h', distance to A 'x', and distance between A and B 'd' (appears in later phases)

interactions.label: Airplane altitude
interactions.teaches: Raising or lowering the airplane while keeping the ground targets fixed changes both angles of depression simultaneously.

interactions.label: Distance between A and B
interactions.teaches: Moving the farther target along the road only changes its specific angle of depression, demonstrating that the two triangles can be analyzed independently despite sharing the height.

interactions.label: Solving phases
interactions.teaches: To solve for unknown distances, the real-world scene is abstracted into a geometric model by dropping a perpendicular altitude and labeling the resulting shared sides and known angles.

demo_steps.title: The Scene
demo_steps.narration: An airplane measures the angles of depression to two points, A and B, on the highway below. These angles are measured downward from the horizontal flight path.

demo_steps.title: Forming Right Triangles
demo_steps.narration: Dropping a perpendicular line from the airplane to the ground creates two right triangles. By alternate interior angles, the angles of elevation from A and B are identical to the angles of depression.

demo_steps.title: Setting up the Equations
demo_steps.narration: Because both triangles share the same vertical height (h), we can write two tangent equations involving h and use them as a system to find the missing ground distances.

demo_steps.title: Changing the Target Distance
demo_steps.narration: If point B is located further down the road, its angle of depression becomes shallower, but the altitude (h) and the inner triangle to point A remain completely unchanged.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because both sight lines originate from the same airplane, they form two overlapping right triangles that share an identical vertical height, creating a constraint that allows solving for the ground distances.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Place the airplane at the top left. Draw a teal dashed horizontal line extending to the right from the plane's nose. Draw the ground line parallel below it. Sight line to A is steeper (49 degrees); sight line to B is shallower (25 degrees). Angle arcs originate from the top horizontal line. When solvePhase transitions to 'Right triangles', fade in a vertical drop line from the plane to the ground, add right angle markers, and add angle arcs at A and B on the ground matching the depression angles. In 'Variables' phase, label the vertical line 'h', the ground segment under the plane to A as 'x', and the segment A to B as 'd'. Slider interactions dynamically update the steepness of the sight lines and the numeric angle labels.

authoredContext:
A pilot is flying over a straight highway. He determines the angles of depression to two mileposts, 2.1 km apart, to be 25° and 49°, as shown in the figure. Find the distance of the plane from point A and the elevation of the plane.

Diagram of a plane flying over a highway. It is to the left and above points A and B on the ground in that order. There is a horizontal line going through the plan parallel to the ground. The angle formed by the horizontal line, the plane, and the line from the plane to point B is 25 degrees. The angle formed by the horizontal line, the plane, and point A is 49 degrees.

The arc for the shallower angle is drawn as a solid line, whereas it is dashed in the source figure.
The generated figure evaluates the shallower angle to 24° by default instead of the 25° shown in the source.
The generated figure includes prominent black dots at points A and B on the ground, which do not appear in the source figure.
